name: Lourdes
cover: Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes
tagline: The grotto of Bernadette, in the foothills of the Pyrenees
summary: In 1858 a young Bernadette Soubirous reported visions of the Virgin Mary in a grotto by the river, and Lourdes became one of the largest Catholic pilgrimage sites in the world. Millions come for the grotto, the healing baths and the nightly candlelit procession, with the high Pyrenees just beyond the town.
seasonNote: The pilgrimage season runs April to October, with the nightly torchlight procession; 15 August (the Assumption) is the busiest day. Many hotels close in winter.
arrival: Tarbes-Lourdes-Pyrénées airport is 15 minutes away; TGV trains from Paris take about 5 hours, and regional trains link Toulouse and Bordeaux.
gettingAround: The town and sanctuary are walkable; buses and taxis run to the mountains.
cashTip: Cards work in most places; carry coins for candles and small offerings.
foodTip: Hearty Pyrenean food: garbure soup, Tarbes beans, local lamb, sheep's cheese and gâteau à la broche cooked on a spit.
buyTip: Rosaries, candles, bottles for the spring water, Pyrenean wool and cheese.
baseArea: Hotels between the old town and the sanctuary

items.name: Sanctuary and Grotto of Massabielle
items.wiki: Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes
items.summary: The grotto where Bernadette saw the Virgin Mary, with the spring, the baths and three basilicas built above it.
items.expect: Free and open to all; queues to touch the grotto wall; quiet is asked near the grotto.
items.tip: Pass through the grotto early morning, and collect spring water from the taps nearby.
items.why: One of the most visited Christian shrines in the world.
flow: Grotto, then the Upper Basilica and the Rosary Basilica.

items.name: Torchlight Marian procession
items.summary: Every evening in season, thousands carry candles from the grotto to the Rosary Basilica, singing the Ave Maria in many languages.
items.expect: Daily at 9pm from April to October; buy a candle with a paper shade.
items.tip: Watch from the ramps above the Rosary Square for the river of lights.
items.why: The most moving moment in Lourdes.
flow: Walk with the procession or watch from above.

items.name: Château fort de Lourdes
items.summary: A medieval castle on a rock above the town, now the Pyrenean museum of folk life.
items.expect: A lift goes up; good views of the sanctuary and mountains.
items.tip: Come for the view over the basilicas.

items.name: Bernadette's places
items.summary: The Boly Mill where Bernadette was born and the 'cachot', the former jail where her poor family lived.
items.tip: Follow the 'In the footsteps of Bernadette' signs through the old town.
items.why: The human story behind the shrine.
flow: The cachot, then the parish church.

items.name: Pic du Jer
items.summary: A 1900 funicular climbs to a summit with views over Lourdes and the Pyrenees.
items.tip: Go on a clear afternoon and walk down.
items.why: The best view of the Pyrenees from town.
flow: Summit, then caves or walk down.

items.name: Cirque de Gavarnie
items.summary: A vast amphitheatre of cliffs and waterfalls, including one of Europe's highest falls.
items.expect: About an hour's drive; a flat walk of an hour each way.
items.tip: Go in June when the waterfalls are full.
items.why: A World Heritage wonder of the Pyrenees.
flow: Walk to the foot of the falls.

items.name: Garbure and Pyrenean cooking
items.summary: A thick soup of cabbage, beans and duck confit, served in old-town restaurants.
items.expect: Simple, hearty menus at fair prices.
items.tip: Order the menu of the day with garbure and lamb.
flow: Pick a bistro in the old town.

items.name: Gâteau à la broche
items.summary: A spiky spit-roasted cake, a speciality of the Pyrenees sold in pâtisseries.
items.expect: Sold by the slice or whole.
items.tip: Buy a small one to take home.

items.name: Tarbes beans and local produce
items.summary: The Halle market sells Tarbes beans, Pyrenean cheeses, charcuterie and honey.
items.tip: Assemble a picnic for the mountains.

name: Fátima
tagline: Portugal's great Marian shrine, near Batalha and Tomar
summary: In 1917 three shepherd children reported visions of the Virgin Mary at Fátima, and the sanctuary is now one of the most important Catholic shrines in the world. Nearby are three World Heritage monasteries at Batalha, Alcobaça and Tomar.
seasonNote: The great pilgrimages fall on 12 and 13 May and 12 and 13 October, when hundreds of thousands arrive, many on foot. Summers are hot; winters quiet.
arrival: Buses from Lisbon take about 90 minutes; Fátima railway station is 20 km away. Lisbon and Porto airports are the closest.
gettingAround: The sanctuary and town are walkable; rent a car or take buses to the monasteries.
cashTip: Cards work widely; carry coins for candles.
foodTip: Roast suckling pig (leitão), bacalhau, and conventual sweets from the nearby monasteries.
buyTip: Rosaries, candles and religious art; Alcobaça ceramics.
baseArea: Hotels and pilgrim houses around the sanctuary

items.name: Sanctuary of Fátima
items.summary: A huge esplanade between the Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary and the modern Basilica of the Holy Trinity.
items.expect: Free and open to all; some pilgrims cross the esplanade on their knees.
items.tip: Attend the evening rosary and candlelit procession.
items.why: One of the great Marian shrines of the world.
flow: Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary.
The esplanade, then the Holy Trinity basilica.

items.name: Chapel of the Apparitions
items.summary: The small chapel on the spot of the apparitions, with the statue of Our Lady of Fátima.
items.expect: Masses throughout the day; candles burn beside it.
items.tip: Join the 9:30pm rosary procession, which begins here.
flow: Light a candle at the burners.

items.name: Aljustrel and the Way of the Cross
items.summary: The hamlet of the three seers' family homes, reached by a path of Stations of the Cross through olive groves.
items.expect: A 2 km walk from the sanctuary.
items.tip: Walk the Via Sacra and visit the Valinhos apparition site on the way.
flow: Walk the Way of the Cross.

items.name: Batalha Monastery
items.summary: A Gothic masterpiece with lacy stone and the roofless 'Unfinished Chapels'.
items.tip: Don't miss the Unfinished Chapels.
items.why: A World Heritage Site and one of Portugal's finest buildings.

items.name: Convent of Christ, Tomar
items.summary: The Knights Templar's castle-convent, with a round church and a famous Manueline window.
items.tip: See the round Charola and the Manueline window.

items.name: Alcobaça Monastery
items.summary: A vast Cistercian monastery with the tombs of the tragic lovers Pedro and Inês.
items.tip: Combine with Batalha and Nazaré in one day.
items.why: A World Heritage monastery with Portugal's great love story.

items.name: Leitão (suckling pig)
items.summary: Crisp roast suckling pig with pepper sauce, a regional favourite.
items.expect: Restaurants on the roads around town.
items.tip: Order with salad and orange slices.

items.name: Bacalhau houses
items.summary: Salt cod cooked a dozen ways in simple family restaurants near the sanctuary.
items.tip: Try bacalhau com natas or à Brás.

items.name: Conventual sweets
items.summary: Egg-yolk and almond sweets first made by nuns, sold in Alcobaça's pastelarias.
items.tip: Try the 'cornucópias' of Alcobaça.

name: Santiago de Compostela
tagline: The end of the Camino, at the tomb of St James
summary: The goal of the Camino de Santiago, Europe's great medieval pilgrimage, and the burial place of St James the Apostle. Pilgrims arrive in the Praza do Obradoiro after weeks of walking to see the cathedral, the swinging botafumeiro and a granite old town of arcades and tapas bars.
seasonNote: Summer is busiest, especially around the feast of St James on 25 July. Galicia is green because it rains often, especially October to April.
arrival: Santiago airport is 20 minutes away; high-speed trains from Madrid take about 3.5 hours; buses connect Porto.
gettingAround: The old town is compact and pedestrian.
cashTip: Cards work everywhere; carry coins for tapas bars.
foodTip: Pulpo a feira (Galician octopus), Padrón peppers, empanada, Albariño wine and almond tarta de Santiago.
buyTip: Scallop-shell souvenirs, Sargadelos ceramics, jet jewellery and Galician cheese.
baseArea: The old town around the cathedral

items.name: Santiago de Compostela Cathedral
items.summary: The Romanesque cathedral over the tomb of St James, with the Portico of Glory and the giant swinging censer.
items.expect: Free entry to the church; book for the Portico of Glory and the roof tour.
items.tip: Check when the botafumeiro will swing (usually at the evening pilgrim Mass and on Fridays).
items.why: The goal of every pilgrim on the Camino.
flow: Tomb of St James, then the roof tour.

items.name: Praza do Obradoiro
items.summary: The great square in front of the cathedral where pilgrims finish their walk.
items.tip: Sit on the stones at midday to watch pilgrims arrive.
items.why: One of the most moving squares in Europe.

items.name: Old town and the Rúa do Franco
items.wiki: Old Town of Santiago de Compostela
items.summary: A World Heritage old town of granite arcades, monasteries and tapas bars.
items.tip: Do a tapas crawl down Rúa do Franco.
items.why: One of Spain's finest old towns.

items.name: Museum of Pilgrimage and Santiago
items.summary: A museum of the history of the Camino and the city.
items.tip: Visit before walking the old town to understand it.
items.why: The story of a thousand years of pilgrims.

items.name: Monte do Gozo
items.summary: The 'Hill of Joy' where pilgrims get their first sight of the cathedral spires.
items.expect: A walk or short bus ride.
items.tip: Walk the last 5 km of the Camino into town from here.
items.why: Feel the final stretch of the Camino.

items.name: Cape Finisterre
items.summary: The rocky cape once thought to be the end of the world, where many pilgrims continue to watch the sunset.
items.expect: About 90 minutes by car or bus.
items.tip: Stay for sunset at the lighthouse.
items.why: The true end of the Camino for many.

items.name: Pulpo a feira
items.summary: Tender octopus with olive oil, paprika and salt on a wooden plate.
items.expect: Served in pulperías across the old town.
items.tip: Order with cachelos (boiled potatoes) and a glass of Ribeiro.

items.name: Mercado de Abastos
items.summary: The city's covered market, where stalls will cook the seafood you buy.
items.tip: Buy shellfish and have it cooked at the market bar.

items.name: Tarta de Santiago
items.summary: An almond cake dusted with sugar around the cross of St James.
items.expect: Sold in every bakery and café.
items.tip: Pair it with a glass of orujo herbal liqueur.

name: Assisi
tagline: St Francis's hill town in green Umbria
summary: The pink-stone hill town of St Francis and St Clare, with the great Basilica of St Francis and its Giotto frescoes. Pilgrims and art lovers come for the churches and the hermitages in the woods, and stay for the quiet Umbrian countryside of olive groves and hill towns.
seasonNote: Spring and autumn are ideal. 4 October, the feast of St Francis, is the busiest day; summers are hot.
arrival: Trains from Rome (about 2 hours) and Florence (about 2.5 hours) stop at Santa Maria degli Angeli, a 10-minute bus below the town. Perugia airport is 15 minutes away.
gettingAround: The hill town is walkable but steep; buses run to the station and the valley.
cashTip: Cards work widely; carry coins for candles and small cafés.
foodTip: Umbrian food: strangozzi pasta with black truffle, torta al testo flatbread, wild boar and Sagrantino wine.
buyTip: Religious art, Franciscan crafts, Deruta ceramics, truffles and olive oil.
baseArea: Inside the old walls near Piazza del Comune

items.name: Basilica of St Francis
items.summary: Two stacked churches over the tomb of St Francis, covered in frescoes by Giotto, Cimabue and others.
items.expect: Free; silence and covered shoulders; no photos inside.
items.tip: Visit the crypt with St Francis's tomb, then the Giotto cycle in the Upper Church.
items.why: A World Heritage Site and a treasury of early Italian art.

items.name: Basilica of St Clare
items.summary: The pink-and-white striped church of St Clare, holding the crucifix said to have spoken to St Francis.
items.tip: See the San Damiano crucifix in the side chapel.
items.why: The story of St Clare and her sisters.

items.name: Eremo delle Carceri
items.summary: The hermitage in the woods where St Francis went to pray, in a peaceful oak forest.
items.expect: A 4 km uphill walk or a short drive.
items.tip: Walk up through the woods and take a taxi back.
items.why: The most peaceful place in Assisi.

items.name: Rocca Maggiore
items.summary: A medieval castle on the hilltop with views over the Umbrian valley.
items.tip: Go at sunset.

items.name: Temple of Minerva and Piazza del Comune
items.summary: A Roman temple facade, now a church, on the town's main square.
items.tip: Have an espresso on the square in the evening.

items.name: Santa Maria degli Angeli
items.summary: A huge basilica built around the tiny Porziuncola chapel where St Francis began his order and died.
items.tip: Visit on arrival or departure by train.

items.name: Spello
items.summary: A flower-filled hill town with Pinturicchio frescoes, 15 minutes away.
items.expect: Steep lanes; famous flower carpets in June.
items.tip: Visit for the Infiorata flower festival at Corpus Domini.

items.name: Truffle pasta trattorias
items.summary: Trattorias serving strangozzi and umbricelli pasta with black truffle.
items.tip: Order strangozzi al tartufo and a glass of Sagrantino.

items.name: Torta al testo
items.summary: Umbrian griddle flatbread filled with ham, cheese or greens.
items.tip: Try it with prosciutto and pecorino.

items.name: Umbrian wine bars
items.summary: Enotecas pouring Umbrian wines with cheese and salumi.
items.tip: Taste Sagrantino di Montefalco and Grechetto.
